title: Posner Spatial Cueing
scopeNote: This keeps the performed experiment and the neutral condition that lets a cueing effect be split in two. The second cue-to-target interval, which the original uses to make the effect reverse into inhibition of return, is the first thing cut: it is a second teaching job. The running table of every block, the worked example and the transfer challenge also stay in the longer version, and the page says so.
summary: A spatial-cueing experiment the learner runs on themselves. A box brightens, then a target appears, sometimes where the cue pointed and sometimes not. Their own reaction times separate the benefit of a valid cue from the cost of an invalid one, against their own neutral baseline.
learningObjectives: Describe the spatial-cueing paradigm and the role of valid, neutral and invalid trials.
Separate a benefit of valid cueing from a cost of invalid cueing using a neutral baseline.
Explain why a valid-minus-invalid difference conceals which of the two produced it.
Distinguish covert orienting from moving the eyes, and say what evidence would be needed to tell them apart.
Recognise browser timing, anticipation cut-offs and small cell sizes as limits on what a classroom block can show.
interactionTypes: six untimed practice trials with feedback after each
a performed cueing experiment of 72 trials with results withheld until the end
a keyboard or button response, never timed out
a chart drawing both effects outward from the learner's own neutral baseline
a full table of the values behind the chart
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Every reaction time is measured and analysed in the browser and is gone when the page is closed.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout: the left and right arrow keys, or two labelled buttons that name the key they duplicate. No trial is ever timed out, so nothing depends on responding within a window. The display carries a description that changes with the trial and names which side the target appeared on, so the task itself is followable without seeing the boxes. Response keys are disabled until a target is showing, which prevents an accidental press being recorded as a response. The result chart carries a description giving all three means and both effects, and every value is repeated in a table. Nothing fades, moves or animates, so there is nothing for a reduced-motion rule to switch off, and the page says so. Each stage is announced through a polite live region.
dataStatus: The learner's own reaction times, produced in the moment. Nothing is a norm and nothing is compared with anyone else.
simulationNotes: The trial is fixation 500 ms, cue 100 ms, a 100 ms gap, then the target until the learner responds, so cue onset to target onset is 200 ms. A third of trials are neutral, both boxes cued; of the cued trials three quarters are valid. The cue therefore has to be worth believing, which is what makes the effect appear and also why the invalid mean rests on the fewest trials. The response is localisation, left or right, as in the original rather than simple detection: a single detection key can be pressed before anything appears, two keys cannot be, so accuracy is meaningful. Responses under 150 ms or over 2000 ms are counted, reported and kept out of the means. Results are withheld until the block ends, because a running condition mean during a speeded block changes how people answer the next trial.
readmeTopic: moving attention without moving the eyes, and why a cueing effect is two effects rather than one
